Q01_HET_ZERO_WIND: Heat-flux heterogeneity drives secondary circulations and stronger PBL thermals.
At 14.4 km and zero wind, patches larger than 5 km support deep precipitating convection over dry patches while homogeneous forcing retains shallow clouds.
Cross-patch mixing makes the dry-patch mixed layer cooler and moister than its homogeneous analogue and reduces the near-surface dry-wet temperature contrast.
Q02_HET_ONE_MS: A 1 m/s wind breaks circulation-front symmetry and moves convergence to the downwind edge.
Clouds initiated over the dry-patch updraft branch advect downwind.
For 14.4 km patches, 1 m/s does not suppress deep-convection transition because the potential circulation is stronger than the imposed wind.
Q03_RONDONIA_REGIMES: Rainy-season cloud and rainfall patterns show little land-cover signature under original or weakened wind.
During the break, weaker wind strengthens land-induced circulations and low cloud but produces little local rain.
On the first dry-season afternoon, weak wind permits shallow and deep convection and broader shifted rainfall; later days lose the land-cover signature.
Q04_DRY_SOIL_CONTRADICTION: Satellite observations favor afternoon rain over locally drier soils in semi-arid regions.
Six models predominantly favor wetter soils.
The model preference is attributed to convective schemes that respond strongly to moist instability over wetter soil.
Q05_FOREST_CLOUD_EDGE: Summer daytime cloud frequency is higher and cloud duration longer over the large forests.
For the larger Landes forest, cloud enhancement concentrates at downwind and cross-wind edges, especially above 1 m/s.
The smaller Sologne forest has no clear wind-edge relation and the forest preference is seasonally restricted.
Abrupt forest removal reduces local summer cloud frequency.
Q06_IRRIGATION_EXTREMES: Irrigation cools annual maximum daytime temperature and shortens heat waves.
It warms annual minimum nighttime temperature, so daytime and nighttime effects have opposite signs.
Q07_GLOBAL_IRRIGATION: Irrigation cools irrigated grid cells but can warm non-irrigated land remotely.
It increases humidity, cloud fraction in summer and autumn, and land precipitation in the simulated global mean.
Q08_AFFORESTATION_HYDROCLIMATE: Afforestation generally increases latent heat, reduces sensible heat, cools near-surface air, and increases precipitation.
Energy-partitioning responses are larger under dry La Nina conditions.
Some shortgrass or soybean conversions reverse sensible-heat and temperature signs during wet El Nino conditions.
Q09_DEFORESTATION_CLOUD_ALBEDO: Deforestation reduces turbulent heat flux and hence uplift and moisture supply, reducing cloud cover.
The loss of cloud warms the surface and offsets roughly 44-50 percent of the cooling from increased surface albedo in the reported analyses.
Q10_RAJASTHAN_TRANSFER: Vegetation and moisture contrasts can motivate hypotheses about thermal gradients, convergence, cloud timing, and downwind edge effects.
The 10-15 km geometry is analogous to a scale-sensitive idealized experiment but is not validated for Rajasthan.
Weak user-stated monsoon wind and derived climatological wind must not be silently reconciled.
The literature does not justify a local rainfall guarantee or cardinal placement without local geometry and WRF or field validation.
